TRELLIS.2 · penguin_circuits · qkvo+sa, rank 4

Warm-Starting the Adapter

Train an adapter on a penguin twice. Once from zero, once starting from an adapter already fitted to a completely different object — a cow. The second run ends 1.00 dB higher, and the gap never closes.

What goes in, and where it comes from

Three inputs. They are easy to confuse, so here they are separated.

InputWhat it isWhere it comes fromWhat it does
MESH penguin_circuits_render_frame_guan.obj the posed penguin, fixed for the whole run decides where the 1,999 latent voxels sit. Never optimised — TRELLIS.2 takes it as an input, it is not generated.
CONDITIONING data/penguin_circuits/frames_from_video/frame_0001…0121.png the 121 frames of kling_penguin_circuits.mp4, cropped and premultiplied becomes DINOv3 tokens [1, 1029, 1024], one set per frame. This is what the cross-attention reads, and the changing conditioning is what makes the texture move.
GT TARGET out/gt_targets_penguin_circuits_guan/frames/gt_0001…0121.png the 2D copy: each video frame stencilled into the mesh's own rasterised silhouette what the loss is scored against. Not the raw video frame — only the pixels that fall inside our silhouette, so the loss is purely texture and never geometry.
The one that is easy to miss

Conditioning and GT target are both derived from the same video but are not the same thing. The conditioning is the raw frame, cropped, fed to DINOv3 as the model's input. The GT target is that frame stencilled into the mesh silhouette, used only to compute the loss. Anything the video shows outside the silhouette never reaches either the loss or the score.

What the LoRA is, and what it is trained on

FrozenTrained
TRELLIS.2-4B texture flowall of it, 30 blocks—
LoRA on cross_attn—to_q, to_kv, to_out
LoRA on self_attn—sa_qkv, sa_out
total trainable—2,334,720 params, rank 4

The adapter is a rank-4 delta — W′ = W + (α/r)·BA with B zero-init, so at step 0 the model is bit-identical to frozen TRELLIS.2. Nothing about the mesh is learned; the adapter only changes what colour the voxels take.

The only difference between the three arms

All three train on the same penguin mesh, the same 121 penguin conditioning frames, the same 121 penguin GT targets, same seed, same 30 epochs.

  • baseline — conditioning crop found by brightness threshold; adapter starts at B = 0
  • + mask crop — crop taken from render_mask.npy instead; adapter still starts at B = 0
  • + warm start — same mask crop, but the adapter starts from spot_lava's finished checkpoint (a cow) rather than from zero
spot_lava's only role

It supplies the starting weights for the warm arm and nothing else. No spot mesh, no spot frames and no spot targets enter any of these runs. Everything trained, evaluated and rendered on this page is the penguin.

What is being compared

Three runs on the same mesh, the same 121 frames, the same recipe. Each step changes exactly one thing from the step above it, so every delta is attributable.

The result Starting from an adapter fitted to a cow and continuing on a penguin beats training the penguin from scratch by +0.998 dB and +0.0129 SSIM. Both runs used the same seed, the same 121 frames and the same 30 epochs — the only difference is where B started.

The gap narrows but does not close

Monitor PSNR, 15-frame subset, warm minus cold.

Warm at epoch 1 already sits above cold at epoch 8. The spot adapter is worth roughly seven epochs of training on an object it has never seen. The gap peaks at epoch 6 and then narrows steadily — but it flattens near +1 dB rather than reaching zero, so this is not merely faster convergence to the same place.

What the run also measured, under the wrong name

A label to fix before anyone reads final_eval.json

Each run records a frozen baseline. But base = evaluate(ALL_FRAMES) runs after GATE-init, and full_inference always wraps in lora_ctx. So in the warm run that number is not frozen TRELLIS.2 — it is spot_lava's adapter applied zero-shot to the penguin.

Which makes it a useful measurement stored under a misleading key:

ArmWhat its frozen field actually holdsPSNRSSIM
baselinetrue frozen TRELLIS.2, brightness crop9.5760.0783
coldtrue frozen TRELLIS.2, mask crop10.8240.2516
warmspot_lava's adapter, zero-shot on the penguin14.8980.5942

Two things fall out. The cow's adapter, applied to a penguin with no training at all, is +4.07 dB and +0.34 SSIM above frozen — transfer quantified, not just shown as video. And the crop fix alone lifts even the frozen baseline by 1.25 dB, which is independent evidence the brightness crop was mis-framing the object.

Why the crop fix was needed

The pipeline had two different answers to “where is the object”, and on this video they disagreed.

targets + loss mask   ->  gt_render_dir/render_mask.npy      (geometry)
conditioning crop     ->  min(RGB) < 245 on the raw frames   (brightness)

union of the brightness mask, measured:
  spot_lava           21.2% of frame   crop 721 px    agree
  horse_metal         16.1%            crop 717 px    agree
  teapot_porcelain    16.4%            crop 716 px    agree
  penguin_circuits   100.0%            crop 959 px    <-- the whole frame
  whale_spots        100.0%            crop 959 px    <-- the whole frame

penguin lights its own background mid-video, so “not near-white” becomes the entire image and the crop stops cropping. Nothing raised — the object was simply conditioned at a different scale from every other run. GATE-crop now refuses any crop wider than 94% of the frame, so this cannot recur silently.

Four fixed cameras

Not an orbit. Each video is a single stationary camera held for all 121 frames, so the only thing that moves is texture. One is the training view; three are angles the adapter was never supervised from.

Why fixed cameras and not a turntable

In a rotating video a texture change and a viewpoint change look the same, so an orbit cannot tell you whether the texture lives on the surface or was fitted to one angle. Four still cameras answer it: if the warm arm holds at 120°, 180° and 240° the way it does at 0°, the adapter wrote to the 3D field rather than to the training view.

How these three angles were chosen

By measuring true silhouette coverage per yaw with a triangle rasteriser, not by defaulting to 90/180/270. On this mesh 90° and 270° are the worst views available — 18.9% and 19.1%, the penguin edge-on. The four used here all sit at 22–24%.

Stated plainly

Before a reviewer finds it
  • One object, one source. spot_lava → penguin_circuits. Whether warm-starting helps in general is not established by a single pair.
  • Two variables move between baseline and warm. The crop fix and the warm start are separated by the middle rung, but the baseline was never re-run with the mask crop and B=0 on the original code path, so the isolation rests on the cold arm being otherwise identical.
  • No held-out set. --held-every is 0; the final evaluation runs over all 121 training frames and the checkpoint is chosen on a subset of the same frames.
  • The first composite was built against half-written renders. My wait loop counted sacct --format=State rows without -X, so each job counted three times (.batch, .extern, main) and it proceeded at 4 of 12 finished. Caught by an assertion on frame counts, not by inspection. The videos above are rebuilt from all 1,452 frames.
  • The zero-shot number is a by-product. 14.898 was recovered from a mislabelled field, not from an experiment designed to measure it. It should be re-run deliberately before it is cited.
